dating_policy: Dates are broad scholarly/conventional ranges and may be uncertain; they are metadata, not proof of an individual inscription's date.

ancient-egyptian.dating: Archaic/Old Egyptian from the late 4th–3rd millennium BCE; Middle Egyptian ca. 2100–1500 BCE; Late Egyptian ca. 1500–700 BCE; Demotic ca. 700 BCE–400 CE; Coptic continues into the first millennium CE.
ancient-egyptian.script_type: logosyllabic / consonantal sign system with semantic and phonetic signs
ancient-egyptian.notes: Hieroglyphic, Hieratic and Demotic are writing traditions used for different contexts; language stage and script are separate dimensions.

akkadian.dating: Attested from the 3rd millennium BCE through the 1st millennium BCE; major literary and administrative phases include Old Akkadian, Old Babylonian, Middle Babylonian, Neo-Babylonian, Old Assyrian, Middle Assyrian and Neo-Assyrian.
akkadian.notes: Akkadian uses a Sumero-Akkadian cuneiform tradition; sign readings are context-sensitive.

sumerian.dating: Written Sumerian is attested from the late 4th millennium BCE; major documented phases include Early Dynastic, Ur III and Old Babylonian literary Sumerian.
sumerian.notes: Sumerian and Akkadian can share the same cuneiform sign inventory while representing different languages.

ugaritic.dating: Primarily late 2nd millennium BCE, especially the Late Bronze Age corpus of Ugarit.
ugaritic.notes: Ugaritic combines an alphabetic inventory with the cuneiform writing technology of the region.

phoenician.dating: Conventional Phoenician alphabet use from about the 11th/10th century BCE through the Hellenistic period; Neo-Punic continued later in North Africa.
phoenician.notes: Direction is normally right-to-left; inscriptional layouts can vary.

ancient-hebrew.dating: Paleo-Hebrew is documented in the Iron Age and Second Temple periods; Biblical Hebrew is principally a first-millennium BCE written language, with later transmission in square Hebrew script.
ancient-hebrew.notes: Paleo-Hebrew and the later square Hebrew script are related but visually distinct writing traditions.

aramaic.dating: Imperial Aramaic is chiefly first-millennium BCE; later varieties include Nabataean, Palmyrene, Hatran and Syriac traditions extending into the Common Era.
aramaic.notes: Aramaic is a language family continuum with multiple historically distinct scripts.

ancient-north-arabian.dating: Broadly first millennium BCE into the early centuries CE; individual traditions have different chronologies and the umbrella classification remains under active revision.
ancient-north-arabian.region: northern and northwestern Arabia, Jordan, southern Syria and adjacent regions
ancient-north-arabian.notes: ANA is a conventional umbrella; Dadanitic, Taymanitic, Safaitic, Hismaic and Thamudic categories should not be treated as one language.

old-south-arabian.dating: Main epigraphic tradition is conventionally dated to the first millennium BCE and early centuries CE, with chronological boundaries varying by corpus and kingdom.
old-south-arabian.notes: Sabaean, Minaean, Qatabanian and Hadramitic are language/corpus traditions associated with the Old South Arabian script.

greek.dating: Mycenaean Greek is attested in the 2nd millennium BCE; alphabetic Greek develops from the late 2nd/early 1st millennium BCE; Classical, Hellenistic and Koine phases span the first millennium BCE and later antiquity.
greek.notes: Ancient Greek has multiple local alphabets before the later standardization of Ionic-derived forms.

latin.dating: Old Latin is attested in the first millennium BCE; Classical Latin is conventionally associated with the late Republic and early Empire; Late and Medieval Latin continue afterward.
latin.notes: Roman inscriptional letterforms vary by period and medium; uppercase/lowercase distinctions are anachronistic for many ancient inscriptions.

chinese.dating: Oracle Bone Script is late 2nd millennium BCE; Bronze and Seal traditions develop through the first millennium BCE; Clerical and later regular/traditional forms follow.
chinese.notes: Script form, historical language stage and modern reading are separate; a character does not have one timeless pronunciation.

japanese.dating: Chinese characters are attested in Japanese contexts by the first millennium CE; Man'yogana, historical kana and later standardized kana develop across antiquity and the medieval period.
japanese.script_type: mixed Han logographs and kana syllabaries
japanese.notes: Classical Japanese, Kanbun and historical kana require period-aware reading rules; modern Japanese TTS is not equivalent to historical pronunciation.

old-persian.dating: Old Persian cuneiform is primarily Achaemenid, conventionally about the 6th–4th centuries BCE.
old-persian.notes: The script was created for Old Persian within a multilingual Achaemenid inscriptional environment.

sanskrit.dating: Vedic Sanskrit is preserved in oral traditions from the 2nd millennium BCE onward; Classical Sanskrit is standardized in the first millennium BCE; manuscripts use many regional scripts across later periods.
sanskrit.script_type: Indo-Aryan language written in multiple Brahmi-derived scripts
sanskrit.notes: Sanskrit is a language, not a single alphabet; script selection is historically and geographically variable.

coptic.dating: Coptic written traditions develop from the Roman period, with major literary corpora from the first centuries CE onward.
coptic.script_type: alphabet derived principally from Greek with Demotic additions
coptic.notes: Sahidic, Bohairic, Fayyumic and Akhmimic are dialect traditions rather than separate alphabets in every sense.

hittite.dating: Hittite cuneiform texts are principally 2nd millennium BCE, with Old, Middle and New Hittite historical stages.
hittite.script_type: Indo-European language written in cuneiform; related Anatolian hieroglyphic tradition for other Anatolian languages
hittite.notes: Hittite cuneiform uses signs inherited from the Mesopotamian writing tradition.

luwian.dating: Luwian is attested in the 2nd and 1st millennia BCE; Hieroglyphic Luwian monuments are especially prominent in the Late Bronze and Iron Ages.
luwian.script_type: language written in cuneiform and Anatolian hieroglyphs
luwian.notes: Cuneiform Luwian and Hieroglyphic Luwian should be modeled as separate script layers.

etruscan.dating: Primarily first millennium BCE, with inscriptions continuing into the Roman period.
etruscan.script_type: alphabet derived from western Greek through Italic transmission
etruscan.notes: Etruscan is usually written right-to-left; boustrophedon occurs in some early contexts.

gothic.dating: Gothic alphabet and written Gothic are principally attested in the 4th–6th centuries CE.
gothic.region: Gothic-speaking communities around the Black Sea and Roman frontier
gothic.notes: The Gothic alphabet is traditionally associated with Wulfila and is strongly influenced by Greek with additional Latin/Runic elements.

old-turkic.dating: Old Turkic runiform inscriptions are chiefly 7th–10th centuries CE, including Orkhon and Yenisei corpora.
old-turkic.notes: Direction can be context-dependent in historical material; modern scholarship often transcribes normalized forms rather than reproducing exact glyph layout.

linear-b-greek.dating: Linear B is principally 14th–13th centuries BCE in Mycenaean administrative contexts.
linear-b-greek.notes: Linear B encodes an early form of Greek with a syllabic orthography and ideographic signs.

cypro-minoan.dating: Cypro-Minoan is broadly Late Bronze Age, approximately the second millennium BCE; reading and language identification remain uncertain.
cypro-minoan.notes: The system is not securely deciphered; translation output must not be represented as established language knowledge.
